item.title: AI, Truth, and Consequences
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

AI, Truth, and Consequences

If artificial intelligence increasingly shapes our decisions, who owns the consequences?

Posted August 24, 2026

Key points
  • AI now joins the reasoning, not just the research, and then steps away from what follows.
  • A human can do 20 percent of the thinking and still own 100 percent of the consequence.
  • Cognition can be shared, but the same may not be said about responsibility.
Source: StartupStockPhotos / Pixabay

There was an old television show called "Truth or Consequences." I remember the name better than I remember much of the show's content, but lately the phrase has taken on a different and even a critical meaning for me. Artificial intelligence (AI) is becoming remarkably good at helping us arrive at answers and decisions. Sometimes it does much more than help. It decides and substantially shapes where we end up. Yet when that techno-decision leaves the screen and enters our real world, something curious happens. The cognition may be shared, but the consequences aren't.

Cognitive Effort and Accountability

Imagine making an important decision with the help of AI. You provide the context, ask some questions, and quickly come to a conclusion. But my bet, borrowed from the ubiquitous 80/20 rule, is that you contributed 20 percent of the actual cognitive work. Not 80 percent, but 20 percent. If the decision turns out brilliantly, you're pleased. If it goes badly, however, the machine doesn't get called into the boss's office.

That asymmetry is fascinating to me and may be one of today's most pressing issues. A human may contribute 20 percent of the cognition and still own 100 percent of the consequence.

Let's start here. Cognition and consequence have typically been close neighbors that share a cognitive border. We rely on all sorts of tools, but the center of intellectual gravity usually remains somewhere inside the person making the decision. Think about a physician confronting a difficult diagnosis. Plenty of other people and sources might inform the decision, but eventually the physician stands accountable. AI complicates this because it doesn't simply hand us information anymore. Increasingly, it participates in the reasoning that turns information into a decision.

To varying degrees, most of us have experienced this. We can begin with an idea or even an intuition, bring it into a conversation with a large language model (LLM). We iterate with AI and often find ourselves in a new and unexpected place. Who thought the final thought? I'm increasingly unsure that the question has a clean answer. Sometimes the cognition seems to emerge from the interaction itself.

Human Responsibility in Decisions Made With AI

But responsibility doesn't become equally fuzzy. In a general sense, AI can't lose its reputation or its job. It can't legitimately apologize to someone harmed by a recommendation or even lie awake wondering how it got something so wrong.

AI can have enormous influence over the cognitive process and almost none of the consequence that follows.

And I think this gets harder as AI gets better. If a machine contributes 5 percent to my reasoning, calling the decision mine seems easy enough. What about 50 percent? What about 80? At some point, we may find ourselves holding people fully responsible for decisions they only partially thought through themselves. Perhaps that's appropriate. Someone still chose to act. But I'm not sure the philosophy of responsibility is quite as simple as the organizational chart might suggest.

We've spent enormous energy asking whether machines can think, reason, understand, or possess something resembling intelligence. Those are fascinating questions. But another question begins after all that thinking is finished.

Who owns a decision when no single mind fully made it?

For now, we can give AI more and more of the cognitive work without giving it any meaningful share of what happens next. The thinking can become distributed across human and machine, while responsibility remains concentrated in one place: us.

item.title: Integrity Is a Choice; It Cannot Be Purchased or Sold
item.description:
Education

Integrity Is a Choice; It Cannot Be Purchased or Sold

Understanding and applying integrity does not guarantee an easy life.

Posted August 24, 2026

Key points
  • Integrity is a choice.
  • Integrity cannot be purchased, sold, or inherited.
  • Integrity, when applied, also enhances and elevates agency.
  • Integrity is a conscious decision and a behavior that is intentional, ethical and moral.
Source: Taoyuetong / Pixabay

Integrity cannot be purchased, sold, traded, negotiated, or acquired through any means. Integrity is a decision and choice that is—in absolute terms—intentional and founded in the principles, practice, and application of ethical and moral behaviors. As such, and irrefutably, integrity is always a choice, regardless of circumstances (Magalhães, 2024).

Declaring that integrity is a choice recognizes that integrity holistically involves the brain, consciousness, the mind, behavior, free will, and the self‑initiated intellectual application of choice. Integrity is not inherited, nor is it granted by circumstance; it is—and it has always been—a self‑determined action of free will (i.e., a choice; Bode et al., 2014; Georgiev, 2021; Magalhães, 2024).

In terms of choice, perhaps the absolute pinnacle of this insight is powerfully expressed by Viktor Frankl. Frankl lived for a time (or perhaps existed for a time) in unimaginable circumstances.

These circumstances led Frankl to write the book Man’s Search for Meaning. As part of this work, Frankl presented the following understanding: “Between stimulus and response there is a space. In that space is our power to choose our response. In our response lies our growth and our freedom” (Frankl, 1946/2006).

From a psychological perspective, research suggests that integrity functions as an internal self‑directed ethical and moral guide. Individuals who maintain consistent ethical and moral values tend to experience less cognitive dissonance, fewer internal tensions, and greater personal positive regard (Cohen & Sherman, 2014; Marcus & Roy, 2019).

This personal positive regard and associated socially presented behavioral consistency can lead to the situation where there is a social belief—within the individual’s associated personal social circle—that they can be trusted and relied upon (Cohen & Sherman, 2014; Marcus & Roy, 2019).

Research indicates that integrity, when applied, also enhances agency. Choosing integrity strengthens the insight that one’s behavior is self‑directed and is not contingent on any external approval considerations. Integrity also affirms that ethical and moral values are not negotiable and that one’s direction in life is a self‑determined conscious choice (Arvanitis & Kalliris, 2020; Frankl, 1946/2006).

Source: Ray_Shrewsberry / Pixabay

In terms of application, integrity is—and has always been—judged by the universal presentation of both words and deeds. This means words must always match and reflect actions. Consequently, integrity is present in how one speaks and acts, and also in how one treats others and how one honors promises and commitments (Arvanitis & Kalliris, 2020; Cohen & Sherman, 2014).

From a broader historical perspective, philosophers such as Socrates, Plato, and Aristotle dedicated their lives and teachings to the disciplined pursuit of truth and to ethical and moral conduct.

During the Renaissance, Michelangelo and Leonardo da Vinci demonstrated that their achievements were also founded in the search for and application of universal principles.

Further to this, Descartes, Bacon, Newton, Locke, and others continued this search for universal truths, which eventually gave rise to the Age of Reason and the Enlightenment.

During this profound social period, integrity in method and inquiry eventually helped establish the scientific method, which continues to this day. Psychology itself is a reflection of this process.

This continual commitment to integrity and the search for universal truths eventually led to the writings of Immanuel Kant and his presentation of the ethical and moral principles of the categorical imperative.

In the categorical imperative, Kant presents what could be described as the social hallmark in the presentation of ethical and moral principles that continue to guide modern law and human rights to this day. In his presentation, Kant insists that for ethical and moral principles to be intrinsically experienced and universally applied, every individual and humanity itself must always be treated as an end in itself and never merely as a means (Kant, 1785/2012; Kant, 1797/1991).

Ultimately, however, no one can impose integrity from the outside. It cannot be bought, borrowed, sold, or inherited. Importantly, choosing integrity does not guarantee an easy life.

item.title: How Philosophical Counseling Can Help
item.description:
Philosophy

How Philosophical Counseling Can Help

Feeling disillusioned, alienated, in an existential crisis, or “lost at sea”?

Posted August 24, 2026

Key points
  • Philosophical counselors help clients with struggles of the human condition that we all face.
  • These include struggles with meaning, purpose, identity, change, belief, integrity, freedom, and authenticity.
  • Philosophical counseling is a collaborative inquiry and practice of "the examined life."

You might have heard the term “philosophical counseling” before, or maybe not. It might seem like a new approach to counseling, but actually it’s as old as philosophy itself. The ancient Greek philosophers saw philosophy not only as an educative activity but also as a kind of therapy for the soul. It helped to ease suffering, develop personal integrity, encourage self-mastery, create justice, and cultivate human flourishing. Philosophy, for the ancients, was a wholly practical endeavor — a “way of life.”

It's true that philosophy in the modern era has become more and more academic as a discipline — more abstract, more esoteric, and more focused on theory disconnected from lived experience. But there have always been traditions in philosophy, even throughout the modern age, that have kept their concern on practical wisdom (for instance, in ethics, political philosophy, environmental philosophy, and existentialism). They have stayed focused on how our thinking can guide our feelings, our actions, our relations with others, and our relations with the other beings of the planet. And they have stayed focused on how we can, as Thoreau put it, “live deliberately.”

Helping Clients With the Philosophical Dimensions of Life Problems

Philosophical counselors (and other philosophical practitioners) take up the ancient practice of philosophy as “the examined life” to help individuals (or groups) with the philosophical dimensions of their own life problems. This might include struggles with meaning and purpose, core beliefs and values, identity and change, social power and injustice, and the quest for integrity, freedom, and authenticity. These are problems of the human condition that we all face, not signs of mental illness.

In my experience, these problems tend to become more “acute” during certain times of life, including:

  • Big life transitions (e.g., starting college, a change of profession, retirement, empty nest, the death of a loved one)
  • Times of disillusionment (in one’s job, sport, relationship, or with regard to traditional hierarchies, values, or pop-culture standards of “success”)
  • Times of alienation (feeling like a stranger in your own home, workplace, or community)
  • Times of feeling “lost at sea” (without direction and unsure about your own priorities and goals)

What Do We Do in a Philosophical Counseling Session?

In a philosophical counseling session, we start by talking through your current life struggles, working to identify and make explicit some of the operating assumptions that are at play in those struggles. Together, we examine your assumptions, consider the effect they are having on you, and consider some alternatives — which might be more subtle, flexible, and empowering. We work to shift your old ways of thinking, and then consider how to put new insights into practice.

article continues after advertisement

A philosophical counselor may draw on any number of philosophical wisdom traditions to help clients open up thinking and try on different frameworks. (Some of my favorite thinkers to draw on are Plato, Aristotle, the Stoics, Kant, Nietzsche, Marx, Sartre, Beauvoir, and Camus.) A philosophical counselor also uses tools of critical and creative thinking that are at the center of their philosophical training, and may draw on personal experience with the big philosophical questions of the ages, as they have shown up in contemporary life.

Philosophical Counseling as a Collaborative Partnership

The Wandering Philosopher
Source: Monica Vilhauer

In the way I practice it, philosophical counseling is a deeply collaborative process, and many of my clients have commented on the nonhierarchical approach we take to discussion. As a philosophical counselor, I am not a doctor or psychotherapist diagnosing and treating a patient, nor a professor lecturing to a student. I am a co-inquirer on a journey with the client to examine their life and the social-political situation in which they live; help them to become aware of their possibilities; help them to find their purpose; and help them develop wisdom, integrity, and empowerment, and create an authentic life. We both bring to the table our own life experiences, experiential wisdom, studies (which can be quite different from each other), and our own thinking abilities. We also bring our curiosity and creativity concerning how to put new insights into practice. In this way, we are thought partners and, if you will, philosophical friends, critically and creatively shaping worldviews and making them concrete in everyday practice.

item.title: What Is the Link Between Climate Change and Child Abuse?
item.description:
Environment

What Is the Link Between Climate Change and Child Abuse?

How a warming world may be increasing the risk of child maltreatment.

Posted August 24, 2026

Key points
  • Extreme heat adds more stress for families struggling with illness, financial strain, or limited resources.
  • Emerging research links climate-related stressors, extreme temperatures, and the risk of child abuse.
  • Climate change may act as a “threat multiplier,” increasing pressures on families and weakening supports.
  • Understanding how climate change affects family life offers new opportunities to prevent child maltreatment.

This post is part 1 of a two-part series.

On one of the hottest days of the summer, I went to Target. It seemed as if every parent in town had had the same idea. Outside, it was miserable. Inside there was air-conditioning, cold drinks, bathrooms, and enough space to wander around for a while. I remember wondering how many families actually needed something and how many were there because Target was cool.

There was a mother shopping with four children, all of them, I guessed, under ten. The kids were restless. One complained. Another wandered off. Someone wanted something. She called them back and asked them to please, please just let her finish shopping.

Then I heard her say, "Shut up."

Not "please be quiet." Not "inside voices." Just a sharp "shut up."

I looked over at her. I wasn't trying to correct her. I was hoping to catch her eye and give her that look parents sometimes give each other. This heat. These kids. I get it.

She looked right back at me, and her face said: Don't you dare.

I knew that look. I'd worn it myself. There is a particular kind of shame in knowing you aren't doing your best parenting and having it happen in public, where everyone can see. Someone trying to "help" can make you feel worse, not better. So I left her alone.

When she turned away, I made a silly face at the youngest child. He looked down.

I saw the family again in the parking lot. By then she was trying to wrangle four hot, cranky children into a hot car. She was opening the windows, trying to get them into car seats and seatbelts, telling someone to stop hitting their sister. Her voice was much sharper than it had been in the store.

And she was crying.

I pulled out my phone and searched for a nearby cooling center. I thought I could mention that I was going there as a way to help her and let her save face. Nothing came up in our town. The closest place I could find was almost 40 minutes away, and I couldn't tell whether it was even open.

So instead, as I loaded my car, I said, "God, this heat is the worst. I hope it breaks soon."

She shook her head.

"Tough day?" I asked, tossing a six-pack of paper towels into the backseat.

"Youngest has an ear infection. We can't go to the town pool. And our apartment AC broke."

"I'm sorry," I said. "That's a lot."

Can Extreme Heat Worsen Parents' Behavior?

I want to be careful here. I didn't see this woman abuse her children. I saw a mother having a very bad day. But I thought about them on the drive home. Mostly I thought about how few choices she had.

And then I wondered: Is there actually a connection between extreme heat, climate change, and child abuse? I didn't know. So I looked.

Turns out, there is.

UNICEF has been studying the intersection of climate change and child protection since 2022. The phrase it uses is "threat multiplier." Climate change doesn't have to directly cause someone to hurt a child to increase the danger around that child. UNICEF's research describes climate shocks worsening poverty, food insecurity and social inequalities while also weakening some of the family and community systems that protect children.

Its initial Kenya research was qualitative and involved more than 500 children, families, and other stakeholders. Families described what happened as droughts and floods made already difficult lives harder. Traditional community and extended-family support systems were breaking down. Participants also described rising stress, anxiety, and depression, often with few mental-health resources available to help.

Then I found research looking specifically at temperature and child maltreatment, including a U.S. study by Mary Evans, Ludovica Gazze, and Jessamyn Schaller. Using child protective services data, they found increases in alleged and substantiated maltreatment involving young children during hot periods. Neglect was the form of maltreatment most sensitive to temperature, and they found some evidence that air-conditioning reduced the association. The study has since been peer-reviewed and published online in The Review of Economics and Statistics.

Air-conditioning. I immediately thought of the woman at Target.

And then I remembered another mother in another parking lot: me.

Coming in part 2: A parking lot in 1989, what psychologists know about heat and family stress, and why climate change may need to become part of the conversation about preventing child maltreatment.
